analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: A bill to eliminate the estate and gift taxes, introduced by a single representative with no cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out three federal taxes on transferring wealth: the estate tax paid by large estates when someone dies, the gift tax on large gifts, and a tax on transfers that skip a generation, such as a grandparent leaving money directly to a grandchild. It applied retroactively to deaths and gifts after December 31, 1997. The bill went nowhere: one sponsor, no cosponsors, and no action after referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The estate tax only applies above a substantial exemption, so repeal would eliminate taxes owed almost exclusively by the wealthiest families when a parent or grandparent dies. Estate-planning lawyers and advisers who sell avoidance services would keep that market, since the tax they help clients avoid would be gone but their role in structuring large transfers would persist.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax entirely, so heirs to large estates would owe nothing on inheritances for deaths after December 31, 1997.
Repeals the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, removing taxes on large lifetime gifts and on transfers that bypass a generation, such as money left directly to grandchildren.
The repeal was written to apply to all deaths and gifts after December 31, 1997, delivering the full benefit immediately rather than phasing it in.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes raise billions of dollars a year, and that revenue comes disproportionately from the wealthiest households; eliminating it means either cutting government services, adding to deficits, or shifting the burden to taxes that fall more broadly on ordinary people.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove billions of dollars a year in federal revenue that comes overwhelmingly from the largest estates, forcing offsetting cuts, more debt, or broader taxes on ordinary households.

The benefit would be extremely concentrated: only estates above the taxable threshold pay the tax at all, so the gain goes to a small share of very wealthy families while the cost is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes.

Supporters' strongest good-faith argument is that the estate tax can force heirs to sell family farms or small businesses to pay the bill, and that it amounts to taxing money that was already taxed as income. That concern is real, but a narrower fix aimed at farms and small businesses would address it without eliminating the tax on the largest fortunes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would flow to heirs of the largest estates, while the cost — lost revenue in the billions annually — would fall on the general treasury and ultimately on ordinary taxpayers. The estate tax touches very few families directly, and mechanisms like the marital deduction and charitable deduction already shield most transfers. The bill made no attempt to target relief at family farms or small businesses; it was a full repeal favoring the largest fortunes.

outcome.mechanism: One representative introduced it, it was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and the committee never acted before the two-year Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Max Sandlin, a Texas Democrat, introduced the bill on November 13, 1997, to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that handles tax legislation.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee never took the bill up, so it never reached the House floor for a vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers came out ahead: the bill died, so the estate tax — which draws revenue disproportionately from the wealthiest estates — stayed on the books. Wealthy families also gained nothing, but they lost nothing they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers; the estate tax survived

for.name: Rep. Max Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; it died in committee without a markup or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the only sponsor was a Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: Full repeal would have spared the largest fortunes billions in estate, gift, and transfer taxes, with the cost shifted to the general treasury. Ordinary families below the taxable threshold would see no direct benefit.

Repeal would end the estate tax that drives much of the demand for their avoidance services, but large family wealth transfers would still need legal and financial structuring. Their revenue would likely shrink.
